extracted.intended_audience: journalists and editors reporting on science and health (science/health reporters, sub-editors, broadcasters)
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practice checklist for preparing, editing and publishing news, features and releases about scientific and health research; focused on accuracy, context, transparency and risk communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask for the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Always identify and check the primary research behind the story: which paper/report, where published, who did the work, and whether it has been peer reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the journal or report, read the methods and results (not just the press release), verify sample size, study design (randomised trial, observational, lab study), endpoints measured and statistical significance. Anti-patterns: reporting only from a press release or quoting headlines without checking the original study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the quality and type of study
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how strong the evidence is given the study type and design — laboratory/animal work, small exploratory studies, observational studies, randomised controlled trials, meta-analyses have different weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain limitations inherent to the design (e.g., animal model vs human trial; correlational vs causal inference). Avoid treating a small or preliminary study as definitive. Look for replication, sample representativeness, controls, blinding, and whether results are likely robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place findings in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the wider scientific and public-health context so readers understand whether results are new, confirmatory, surprising or incremental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the study to existing evidence, quote independent experts about how the new work fits into the overall picture, and explain how likely findings are to change practice or behaviour. Avoid implying that a single paper settles a broad question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify and explain risk clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the story involves risk or benefit, report absolute as well as relative figures and use plain numbers so the audience can judge the scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give baseline rates, number-needed-to-treat/harm where appropriate, and avoid relying solely on relative percentages that exaggerate effect sizes. Use examples/analogies to make scale understandable and highlight uncertainty in estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be accurate about causation vs correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim causal relationships where the study only shows association; state clearly when links are correlational and what further evidence would be required to infer causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for authors' own cautious language, check whether confounding factors were addressed, and avoid headlines/lede sentences that imply cause when the evidence does not support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek independent comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Get reaction from experts who are not part of the study to comment on validity, significance and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose commentators with relevant expertise and no close conflicts of interest; where possible provide more than one independent voice. Use their quotes to counterbalance claims made by authors or press releases and to explain technical points to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for conflicts of interest and funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and report who funded the research and any author affiliations or commercial links that might bias the work or its interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose declared funding sources, industry involvement, consultancies, patent interests and tell readers if any important COIs are not properly declared. If a study is industry-funded or authors have commercial interests, note this as it can affect interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report limitations and uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the study's limitations, uncertainties and unanswered questions explicit rather than burying caveats later in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain methodological weaknesses, uncertainties around measurements or generalisability, and whether results could be due to chance or bias. Avoid presenting provisional findings as established facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with wording, headlines and visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sensationalist or misleading headlines, over-claiming terms (e.g., 'cure', 'miracle'), and visuals that exaggerate effect sizes; ensure the lead sentence accurately reflects the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft headlines and leads that match the body of the story; ensure charts and images are not distorted (e.g., axes start at zero where appropriate) and that infographics explain absolute numbers and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of communication and source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat peer-reviewed publications, preprints, conference abstracts, press releases and regulatory statements differently and make clear to readers which type is being reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reporting on a press release, preprint or conference presentation, explicitly state that the work has not been through peer review (if applicable) and note what that implies about certainty. Do not rely solely on institution PR for technical claims—verify with the study or independent experts.
